fields.claim_quote: If \( G \) contains a cyclic subgroup of order \( m \), then there exists a permutation \( \sigma \in G \) corresponding to a cycle of length $m$ in \( \Gamma \).
fields.explanation: The original three-vertex path and its two edge transpositions are preserved. Mathlib SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet constructs exactly that graph; Subgroup.closure of all its edge transpositions defines the source-generated group. The product sigma of the two swaps belongs to this closure and has order three. Its Mathlib zpowers subgroup is cyclic, contained in the generated group, and has Nat.card three. For every graph walk, IsCycle would force length at least three while IsTrail bounds length by the graph's two edges. Hence no graph cycle exists, in particular no length-three cycle. The surrounding stored source explicitly uses the converse to assert a cycle in the input graph.
fields.flaw: A cyclic subgroup of order m in the group generated by the input graph’s edge transpositions implies that the input graph contains a cycle of length m.
fields.problem: Title: Computational Complexity of Finding Subgroups of a Given Order
fields.source_context:
0143 | 
0144 | 	The subgroup generated by \( \sigma \), denoted \( H = \langle \sigma \rangle \), is a cyclic subgroup of \( G \) of order \( m \):
0145 | 
0146 | 	\[
0147 | 	H = \{ \sigma^0, \sigma^1, \dots, \sigma^{m-1} \}.
0148 | 	\]
0149 | 	Thus we see the equivalence:
0150 | 
0151 | 
0152 | 
0153 | 	\begin{itemize}
0154 | 		\item If \( \Gamma \) has a cycle of length $m$, then \( G \) contains a cyclic subgroup of order \( m \).
0155 | 		\item If \( G \) contains a cyclic subgroup of order \( m \), then there exists a permutation \( \sigma \in G \) corresponding to a cycle of length $m$ in \( \Gamma \).
0156 | 	\end{itemize}
0157 | 
0158 | 
0159 | 	The construction of \( G' \) requires at most \( O(n^2) \) operations, which is polynomial in the input size. The problem of finding a cycle of length $k$ can be shown to be NP-Complete by a reduction from Hamiltonian Cycle problem \cite{alon1997finding}. Checking for a cyclic subgroup of order \( n \) in \( G' \) would then solve the problem of finding  cycle of length $m$ in polynomial time, proving \textsc{NP-hardness} for the problem of finding cyclic subgroup of specified order. Thus the general problem of finding a subgroup of specified order is also NP-Hard.
0160 | 
0161 | 	Now given a subset of elements, we can verify in polynomial time whether it forms a subgroup of order $k$. This involves checking:
0162 | 	\begin{enumerate}
0163 | 		\item The subset has exactly $k$ elements.
0164 | 		\item It is closed under the group operation (using the Cayley table).
0165 | 		\item It contains the identity and each element has an inverse in the subset.
0166 | 	\end{enumerate}
0167 | 	Since each check takes at most $O(k^2)$ time using the Cayley table, the problem is in NP. Thus this problem is NP-complete.
fields.witness: Let m=3 and Γ have vertices {1,2,3} and edges {{1,2},{2,3}}. Its edge transpositions are (12),(23), so G=⟨(12),(23)⟩. The product σ=(12)(23) is a 3-cycle (orientation depends on composition convention), hence H={id,σ,σ²}≤G is cyclic of order 3. But Γ is a path, hence has no graph cycle, particularly none of length 3.
